title: Inference migration escape-hatch — seller deck (draft)
content:
Context and one-line: quick 8-slide sales enablement deck for SEs to run a migration pilot with a clear escape hatch (canary + fallback) so product teams feel safe moving from legacy endpoints to Redwood. Draft — rough speaker notes and visual sketches, NOT finalized.

Audience: platform engineers, infra/platform architects, SREs evaluating a migration to Redwood Dedicated or Private. Typical meeting length: 20 minutes + 15m Q/A.

Slide 1 — Title + framing
- Title: Migration escape-hatch: keep traffic flowing while you switch to Redwood
- Visual: split-screen — left: legacy endpoint (icons: queue, CPU spikes, manual scripts), right: Redwood (icons: routing, cache, canary)
- Speaker note: short opener — "If the pilot goes sideways, you need an escape hatch. This deck shows how to run a safe canary and automated fallback so stakeholders sleep at night."

Slide 2 — Problem we hear from platforms
- Bullet points (pain): unpredictable latency under burst, cost spikes during peak, lack of predictable fallbacks, org risk aversion to cutover windows
- Quick quote: "We can't risk degrading customer-facing latency during pilot." — Platform lead, fintech prospect
- Speaker note: empathize, align: our win is reducing risk not just cost.

Slide 3 — High-level escape-hatch idea (one-liner)
- One-liner: Canary to Redwood with automated, policy-driven fallbacks back to legacy endpoints + observable SLO guardrails
- Visual: flowchart (small): traffic split -> canary -> monitor -> if fail -> fallback route -> alert + rollback
- Speaker note: highlight repeatable ops patterns rather than one-off runbooks.

Slide 4 — Tactical checklist for SE-led pilot (actionable)
- Preflight: data classification, traffic sniff, baseline metrics (p50/p95 latency, error budget remaining), define canary traffic % and duration
- Canary runbook: 1) route 1-5% traffic for 1 hour, 2) verify latencies + token-cost delta, 3) run synthetic golden-queries every 2m, 4) evaluate quality metrics (quick eval subset)
- Escape conditions (fail fast): latency > baseline + 30% for 3 consecutive 1-min windows OR error rate > 2x baseline OR quality regression > threshold
- Fallback actions: immediate 100% reroute to legacy, mark canary as blocked in the console, create incident with runbook link
- Speaker note: sellers should read each item as a checklist to hand to SRE.

Slide 5 — Example signals and quick thresholds (starter set)
- Latency: p95 > baseline*p1.3 over 3 mins -> trigger
- Cost: per-token billing spike > 2x expected for canary window -> alert ops (not automatic fallback)
- Correctness: embedding similarity drop or n-gram overlap < 0.85 on golden set -> block
- Throughput: queue depth growth > 50% sustained -> investigate
- Visual: small table sketch.
- Speaker note: emphasize customizable thresholds; this deck gives initial defaults we use with enterprise pilots.

Slide 6 — Seller playbook: objection responses and ROI snippets
- Objection: "We'd rather do a big-bang cutover." Response: "Big-bang risks user impact; canary + escape hatch gets you confidence and measurable rollback path. Faster to production, lower overall risk."
- Objection: "Will rolling back break anything?" Response: "All routing is stateless and performed at the edge / API gateway layer; rollback is traffic-level only and tests for idempotency before switching fully."
- ROI snippet: For an example mid-market customer, measured 25% lower token-costs within 30 days by enabling caching + quantized model variant; pilot time-to-rollback negligible compared to traditional migration windows. (call out: anonymized reference available)
- Speaker note: quick 30s counters for SEs; hand to AE as pre-read.

Slide 7 — Real-world mini-case: 'EduTech pilot' (anonymized)
- Context: education product routing Q/A at 50 req/s, tight p95 SLA 300ms
- Approach: 2% canary, synthetic golden set, 24h extended run with incremental ramp to 10%
- Outcome: No user-facing errors, p95 improved by 12ms after KV-cache tuning, cost neutral during canary (lower after caching)
- Lessons: synthetic probes caught a tokenizer edge-case early; golden set is critical
- Speaker note: this is a short success vignette to build credibility.

Slide 8 — Next steps / play handoff
- Seller CTA: schedule technical handshake (30m), share baseline metric snapshot (CSV or dashboard export), agree on golden queries (5-10), pick canary window
- Ops CTA: link to runbook + automation repo (private PR), suggest SE checklist itemization for SRE
- Follow-ups / TODOs (internal): adapt default thresholds for regulated verticals, prepare a one-pager for Legal re: data residency assumptions
- Speaker note: leave with clear next action — set meeting and collect baseline metrics.

Appendix (notes to self / engineering asks)
- Engineering needs: quick API toggle endpoint for on-the-fly reroute; small webhook that marks canary as blocked for dashboard integration (ticket to infra: JIRA-1699)
- Product ask: add a "block canary" boolean to rollout API and surfaced in Console (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/console#241)
- Testing note: include a short synthetic harness that can run golden queries against both legacy and Redwood concurrently and output per-query diffs (prototype in repo/ops/synthetics/golden-runner)

Rough slide timing and delivery notes
- 4 min framing + problem, 6 min checklist & signals, 4 min case study + objections, 6 min Q/A and next steps (total 20 + Q/A)

Unresolved / open questions (for product/engineering alignment)
- Should fallback be automatic on cost spikes or only on latency/quality? (ops preference: manual for cost spikes)
- How to safely test stateful endpoints? current deck assumes stateless inference routes; need variant for multi-turn sessions (engineering input required)

Quick sticky points for sellers (soundbites)
- "We guarantee a safe rollback path — pilot risk is operationally bounded."
- "Golden queries are your canary's oxygen: pick them wisely."
- "Canary is not a stunt — it's a measurable experiment we run with your SREs."
